title: Climate change, bank liquidity and systemic risk
summary: This ECB Working Paper uses transaction-level repo market data from 2019-2022 to examine how banks' exposure to climate transition risk affects borrowing costs. The paper finds that banks with higher financed emissions (proxied by greenhouse gas emissions of borrowers) pay 7-12% higher repo rates per standard deviation increase in exposure. This "carbon premium" reflects both a risk premium for credit risk and an "inconvenience premium" from dealer banks' sustainability preferences. The premium triples during periods of market stress, suggesting climate risks amplify systemic vulnerabilities.
key_points: Banks with higher financed emissions pay 7-12% higher repo rates per one standard deviation increase in transition risk exposure
The carbon premium is a combination of (1) risk premium compensating for increased credit risk and (2) "inconvenience premium" reflecting sustainability preferences of dealer banks
The premium triples in size during periods of market stress, indicating climate risks amplify existing financial vulnerabilities
High-emission banks experience faster repo rate adjustments to central bank rate hikes, suggesting uneven monetary policy transmission across the banking sector
Data covers 46 MMSR-reporting European banks with daily repo market volumes of EUR 500-1,500 billion
Transition risk is distinguished from physical risk as the more near-term financial threat to financial institutions
why_it_matters: This research demonstrates that climate transition risk is already materializing in core funding markets, not just equity or bond markets. For policymakers, the findings suggest that (1) climate risk-induced frictions in the repo market could undermine financial stability measures, and (2) monetary policy transmission may be uneven across banks depending on their climate exposure profile. For market participants, the "inconvenience premium" indicates that sustainability preferences of major dealers are becoming a structural factor in repo pricing.
macro_context: The paper contributes to understanding how climate transition risk affects monetary policy transmission. High-emission banks show faster rate pass-through to repo markets, suggesting climate segmentation could create differential policy effects across the banking sector. This has implications for the ECB's ability to uniformly transmit policy rates through the financial system.
market_structure_context: The research reveals that transition risk creates rate segmentation in the repo market based on financed emissions. The "inconvenience premium" term captures how dealer banks' sustainability preferences price out carbon-intensive borrowers independent of credit fundamentals. This represents a structural change in how repo market liquidity is allocated, with implications for bank funding costs that cannot be explained by traditional factors like collateral quality or counterparty relationships.
important_numbers: 7-12% repo rate increase per 1 standard deviation increase in financed emissions
3x (tripling of) carbon premium during market stress periods
EUR 500-1,500 billion daily repo market volume
